name: Umar Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Umar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. I'm going to describe five pictures of how AI might change work and ask how you'd react. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, that's fine. I'm Umar, I'm 43, and I'm a second-year apprentice carpenter, which still sounds funny to say at my age. Before this I drove a forklift in a parcel warehouse for nineteen years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. Before the pictures, tell me about a normal working day for you. What do you actually do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now we're building a new wing on the hospital, so it's stud walls, door frames, boxing in pipes, that kind of thing. I'm on site by half six, I check my list in my little notebook, and Gerry, the old joiner I work under, tells me what I got wrong yesterday. I like the smell of the timber and the fact that at the end of the day there's a wall that wasn't there this morning. What wears me out is my knees, and being the slowest one on the gang when I'm older than half of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, told you so. The warehouse brought in picking robots in 2023 and everyone acted like it was the future, and here we'd be with AI mostly just writing emails. At the union branch I'd probably make a joke about it over tea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means I can breathe. I went through one round of machines taking my job already, and I took the redundancy money and started again at forty. If AI turns out to be hype, then I picked the right trade for once in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd finish my apprenticeship, sit my ticket in about eighteen months and keep paying a bit extra off the mortgage each month like we do now. Maybe I'd stop reading the news about it, because it winds me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. A bit like when the doctor says the lump is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it winds you up. What exactly winds you up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The way people talk about it like weather, like nobody's deciding anything. Somebody decided to put robots in that warehouse, and it was the same people who'd been squeezing our breaks down to twenty minutes. So even if AI fizzles, I'd still want the union keeping an eye on the bosses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids about it at dinner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia's twelve and she uses those chat apps for homework, so she'd probably laugh at me. I'd tell her, see, people still need a carpenter to hang a door. Tomas is nine, he'd just want to know if robots are still coming, because he likes robots, the traitor.

S0.say: I'd tell people at the union branch that I told them so, and that AI turned out to be mostly emails and chat apps. I'd make a joke of it over tea.
S0.think: It means I can relax, because I already lost one job to machines and retrained at forty. If AI fizzles, I picked the right trade for once.
S0.do: Finishes his apprenticeship and sits his carpentry ticket in about eighteen months. Keeps paying a bit extra off the mortgage each month and stops reading AI news.
S0.feel: Relieved, like getting good news from a doctor, with a leftover distrust of bosses.
S0.quote: If AI turns out to be hype, then I picked the right trade for once in my life.
S0.fieldNote: Umar's whole view runs through the warehouse that automated him out in 2023. Even good news is framed as a fight with bosses, not with technology itself. He's at ease in this picture but quick to bring up the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need the union at the table before any of this comes on site, not after. Last time we heard about the robots the week they were delivered. I'd probably post that on the branch group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me more than I'd let on. I'm slow, I'm still learning, and if a machine starts cutting the studs or fixing plasterboard, the first one they let go is the apprentice who's 43. Gerry's got thirty years of skill to fall back on. I've got two years and a notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting, which I mostly do anyway, and push for a deal on new kit: training first, no forced redundancies. I wouldn't go learning AI stuff on my own, that's not me. I'd keep my head down, get my ticket and keep the savings where they are, about ten months of bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicking, but like hearing a noise downstairs at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd push for training, but you wouldn't learn the AI stuff yourself. Isn't that a bit of a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, maybe. If the company trains me on site, on their time, I'll do it, I'm not stupid. What I won't do is sit at home at night watching videos on my phone to make myself cheaper for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The younger lads who live week to week, like Kofi, who's got a baby and rents. I've got Rosa's wage from the hospital and the redundancy money tucked away. If anyone gets hurt by this, it's him before me, and that's not fair either.

S1.say: I'd say the union needs to be at the table before any new kit arrives, not after. Last time we heard about the robots the week they turned up.
S1.think: Privately he's more scared than he'd show, because a slow 43-year-old apprentice is the first to go if machines take over basic tasks. He has two years of skill, not thirty.
S1.do: Goes to every union meeting and pushes for a deal on new equipment with training first and no forced redundancies. Keeps his head down, finishes his ticket and leaves his ten months of savings untouched.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a noise downstairs at night, but not panicking.
S1.quote: Gerry's got thirty years of skill to fall back on. I've got two years and a notebook.
S1.fieldNote: Umar will accept training on company time but refuses to learn AI on his own time, which he sees as making himself cheaper. His worry about being the oldest, slowest apprentice is sharp and personal. He turns quickly to colleagues with less money than him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a choice, not a storm, and the government needs to stop it or slow it. I'd be at every rally, I'd be on the branch chat all day. I'd say, tax the companies that own the robots and pay the people they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really? It means I'm finished as a carpenter before I've even started. I'd be 45, with a trade I'm only half good at, and the robot would be better than me at the one thing I gave up nineteen years to learn. I've done the starting-over thing once and I don't have another one in me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stop every extra cost straight away: the holiday we'd booked, the second car, the kids' swimming would stay but the rest goes. Put every spare bit against the mortgage so the house is safe. Join whatever the union organises, strikes, marches, the lot, and vote for whoever promises to share the money out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Proper sick, like I'd be lying awake doing sums at three in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long. What would you be doing in those two years while you see it coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, not retraining, because retrain as what? If the machine can do everything, there's no ladder to climb. I'd spend those two years trying to make the house ours outright, and fighting, because fighting is the only thing that's worked for people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Rosa that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, we'll be all right, we've got money put by, which is true for a year or two. Then I'd go out to the shed and sit there for a bit. She's a nurse, she'd probably keep her job longer than me, and I don't know how I'd feel about that.

S2.say: I'd say this is a choice made by companies, not a storm, and that government must slow it down and tax the robot owners to pay the people replaced. I'd be at every rally.
S2.think: Privately he thinks it ends his carpentry before it properly starts, at 45 with a half-learned trade. He doesn't feel he has another fresh start in him.
S2.do: Cuts the holiday and the second car straight away and puts every spare bit against the mortgage. Joins every union action and votes for whoever promises to share the gains.
S2.feel: Sick with worry, lying awake doing sums at three in the morning.
S2.quote: the robot would be better than me at the one thing I gave up nineteen years to learn.
S2.fieldNote: With only two years, Umar sees no point retraining because there's no new ladder to climb. His answer is to protect the house and fight. The moment in the shed, and his mixed feelings about Rosa outlasting him at work, said more than his rally talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast one, but I'd say we've got five years to get laws in place, so no excuses. I'd be saying it at the branch and to anyone at the pub who'd listen. Robots on site should come with rules, like scaffolding does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's still the end of the job, just with a bit of a run-up. In five years I'd be 48, and I'd have my ticket and a few years' proper experience, so maybe I'm the one they keep to check the robot's work. Five years is long enough to pay the house off, but not long enough to stop feeling like a spare part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, nothing flash: I'd get my ticket, keep working every hour I can and up the overpayments on the mortgage so we're clear by the time it lands. I'd stand for branch rep, which I've been dodging. When it arrives, I'd fight for a proper redundancy deal for everyone, not just the lucky few.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less sick than the two-year one, but it'd sit on me every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years actually change for you, compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mostly. We've got about ten months put by now, and with five years of Rosa's wage and mine we could pay off the house, and then a lot of the fear goes. It doesn't change what I do for a living, though, it just changes how hard the landing is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stand for branch rep. Why now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if I've got five years' warning and I just sit there, that's on me. Gerry always says you don't get to moan about the job if you never go to the meeting. And I'd rather be in the room when they decide which of us goes.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough time to get laws in place, so there are no excuses. Robots on site should come with rules, like scaffolding does.
S3.think: He thinks it's still the end of the job, just with a run-up. Five years is enough to pay off the house but not enough to stop him feeling like a spare part.
S3.do: Gets his ticket, works every hour he can and raises mortgage overpayments to be clear in five years. Stands for union branch rep and, once AGI arrives, fights for a fair redundancy deal for the whole gang.
S3.feel: Anxious every day, though less sick than in the two-year picture.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to pay the house off, but not long enough to stop feeling like a spare part.
S3.fieldNote: For Umar the extra time changes money, not identity: he'd use it to clear the mortgage, not to learn anything new. Standing for branch rep is a real shift for him. He still frames everything as who's in the room when decisions get made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and if the politicians waste it, they should all be sacked. We could have a proper plan, like guaranteed pay for people whose jobs go. I'd say that loudly, because loud works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is my whole carpentry career, start to finish. I'd be 53 and I'd have done a decade on the tools, paid the house off, and maybe I'd be ready to stop anyway with these knees. I'd be the last carpenter who learned the job, and the first one to watch it go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same plan, slower: get the ticket, clear the mortgage in seven or eight years, keep the rainy-day money. I'd keep going to meetings and push for the union to win a share of what the robots earn. I wouldn't learn to run the machines myself, I'd leave that to the youngsters who like screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's far enough away that I could mostly forget it, except when I'm lying in bed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people would use ten years to switch into a whole new field. Why not you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I already switched, and it took everything. I went from forklift to apprentice at forty and I was the joke of the site for six months. I'm not doing that again at 50 to be the oldest robot-minder in the class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Nadia and Tomas? Would ten years change your plans for them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them in something with people, like Rosa. Nursing, teaching, I don't know. I'd tell them not to bet their life on a job a machine can learn, which is a funny thing to hear from a man who just did exactly that.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift, and politicians who waste it should be sacked. There should be a proper plan, like guaranteed pay for people whose jobs go.
S4.think: He thinks ten years is his whole carpentry career, start to finish, and he'd be ready to stop at 53 anyway. He sees himself as the last carpenter to learn the job and the first to watch it go.
S4.do: Gets his ticket, clears the mortgage in seven or eight years and keeps his rainy-day money. Keeps going to union meetings and pushes for workers to get a share of what the robots earn.
S4.feel: Uneasy in the background; easy to forget in the day, harder at night.
S4.quote: I'm not doing that again at 50 to be the oldest robot-minder in the class.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lines up neatly with Umar's working life, so this picture almost feels survivable. He flatly refuses another career switch because the last one cost him so much pride. His advice to his kids about people jobs comes with a self-aware laugh.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: That's all five. Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. What would actually help is a law that says if a company replaces you with a robot, they keep paying you a share of what you earned for a few years, and the union gets a say in how fast it happens. And keep the hospital open for Rosa.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how it felt the first time, with the warehouse. It felt like being told you were a cost, not a person. If this happens again, I'd just like somebody in charge to remember there's a person with a notebook and bad knees at the other end of it.

headlineQuote: I'd be the last carpenter who learned the job, and the first one to watch it go.
portrait: Umar Diaz is a 43-year-old second-year apprentice carpenter on a hospital build, who drove a forklift in a parcel warehouse for nineteen years until picking robots arrived. He took the redundancy money, retrained at forty, and is now the oldest and slowest on his gang, learning from an old joiner called Gerry. He's a firm union man who blames bosses' choices rather than the technology, and he refuses to learn AI on his own time. He's calm if AI fizzles, uneasy about steady change, and alarmed by AGI in two years; more warning time mostly lets him pay off the house rather than change who he is.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd be 45 with a half-learned trade and no energy for another fresh start.
whatWouldHelp: A law making companies keep paying people they replace with robots for a few years, and a union say in how fast the change happens.
